import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 503

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/503](https://www.erdosproblems.com/503)
-/

namespace Erdos503

open scoped EuclideanGeometry

/--
What is the size of the largest $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ such that every three points from $A$
determine an isosceles triangle? That is, for any three points $x$, $y$, $z$ from $A$, at least two
of the distances $|x - y|$, $|y - z|$, $|x - z|$ are equal.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 51]
theorem erdos_503 (n : ℕ) :
    IsGreatest {(A.ncard) | (A : Set (ℝ^n)) (hA : A.IsIsosceles)} answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

/--
When $n = 2$, the answer is 6 (due to Kelly [ErKe47] - an alternative proof is given by Kovács [Ko24c]).

[ErKe47] Erdős, Paul and Kelly, L. M., Elementary Problems and Solutions: Solutions: E735. Amer. Math. Monthly (1947), 227-229.
[Ko24c] Z. Kovács, A note on Erdős's mysterious remark. arXiv:2412.05190 (2024).
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 51]
theorem erdos_503.variants.R2 :
    IsGreatest {(A.ncard) | (A : Set ℝ²) (hA : A.IsIsosceles)} 6 := by
  sorry

/--
When $n = 3$, the answer is 8 (due to Croft [Cr62]).

[Cr62] Croft, H. T., $9$-point and $7$-point configurations in $3$-space. Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) (1962), 400-424.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 51]
theorem erdos_503.variants.R3 :
    IsGreatest {(A.ncard) | (A : Set ℝ³) (hA : A.IsIsosceles)} 8 := by
  sorry

/--
The best upper bound known in general is due to Blokhius [Bl84] who showed that
$$
|A| \leq \binom{n + 2}{2}
$$

[Bl84] Blokhuis, A., Few-distance sets. (1984), iv+70.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 51]
theorem erdos_503.variants.upper_bound (n : ℕ) :
    ∀ m ∈ {(A.ncard) | (A : Set (ℝ^n)) (hA : A.IsIsosceles)}, m ≤ (n + 2).choose 2 := by
  sorry

/--
Alweiss has observed a lower bound of $\binom{n + 1}{2}$ follows from considering the subset of
$\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}$ formed of all vectors $e_i + e_j$ where $e_i$, $e_j$ are distinct coordinate
vectors. This set can be viewed as a subset of some $\mathbb{R}^n$, and is easily checked to have
the required property.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 51]
theorem erdos_503.variants.lower_bound (n : ℕ) :
    (n + 1).choose 2 ≤ sSup {(A.ncard) | (A : Set (ℝ^n)) (hA : A.IsIsosceles)} := by
  sorry

end Erdos503

reformulations.difference: Maximizes natural-valued `Set.ncard` over nonempty isosceles sets, without an explicit finiteness condition. The source asks for the largest cardinality of an isosceles subset.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Singletons are admissible, so excluding the empty set cannot change the maximum. If the natural cardinalities have greatest element k, an infinite admissible set would contain an admissible finite subset of size k+1, contradicting maximality. Thus the statement enforces finiteness and ordinary cardinality bounds despite `ncard` assigning zero to infinite sets. `Review503.greatest_iff_full_source` proves equivalence to an attained finite cardinality k together with an extended-cardinality bound on every admissible set, allowing the empty set.

reformulations.difference: Uses the same nonempty-set, natural-cardinality maximum encoding for the planar answer 6.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Specializing the generic maximum equivalence to ℝ² and k=6 gives a finite six-point isosceles configuration and an extended-cardinality bound of six on all admissible sets. An infinite counterexample would supply a seven-point counterexample; excluding the empty set is immaterial.

reformulations.difference: Uses the same nonempty-set, natural-cardinality maximum encoding for the three-dimensional answer 8.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Specializing the generic maximum equivalence to ℝ³ and k=8 gives a finite eight-point isosceles configuration and an extended-cardinality bound of eight on all admissible sets. An infinite counterexample would supply a nine-point counterexample; excluding the empty set is immaterial.

reformulations.difference: Bounds every value in the set of admissible `ncard`s rather than explicitly asserting finiteness and bounding ordinary cardinality.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: A uniform natural-cardinality bound N rules out infinite admissible sets: any such set contains an admissible finite subset of size N+1. Conversely, an extended-cardinality bound implies the natural-cardinality bound. The empty set contributes only the automatic inequality 0 ≤ N. This exact equivalence is proved as `Review503.bound_iff_full_source`, and applies with N = (n+2).choose 2.

reformulations.difference: Expresses the lower bound using a supremum in ℕ rather than directly asserting existence of a sufficiently large finite configuration.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The cardinality family is nonempty because it contains 1, and Blokhuis's established upper bound makes it bounded above. A nonempty bounded set of naturals has an attained supremum. Therefore the displayed inequality is equivalent to existence of a finite isosceles set with at least (n+1).choose 2 points. `Review503.lower_iff_full_source` proves this equivalence under the boundedness hypothesis; the unbounded-supremum default value is consequently irrelevant here.

review.notes: All five declarations match the cited source. Its newer lower bound (n+1).choose 2 + 1 does not invalidate the older Alweiss bound stated in the file. Lean checks confirmed the Euclidean metric, empty/singleton/pair behavior, repeated-point equivalence, and maximum 1 in dimension zero. Computable tests of the coordinate-pair construction passed for dimensions 0–6. Scratch files in /workspace/review/ compiled successfully; the equivalence proofs use no sorry axioms or problem theorems. Croft's original article and the linked OEIS entry were inaccessible, but the three-dimensional value is explicit on the main cited source. No repository files were edited.
